evidence: Cic. Lael. 15: memoriam spērō sempiternam fore (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: What one hopes for in the accusative, or in an accusative and infinitive, usually future (spērō tē ventūrum esse). Ut spērō, “I hope”, is said in passing: sed, ut spērō, valēbis (Cic. Att. 7.2.6).

evidence: Cic. Att. 9.10.3: ut aegrōtō, dum anima est, spēs esse dīcitur
terms.comment: Spem habēre, have hope; losing it is dēspērāre (Traupman 154).

phrases.latin: jam tē vidēbō et quidem, ut spērō, dē viā rēctā ad mē
phrases.english: I’ll see you soon, and straight from the road to my house, I hope

phrases.latin: nātō fīliō pater spem dē illō prīmum quam optimam capiat
phrases.english: when a son is born, let the father first form the highest hopes of him

phrases.latin: dēsine fāta deum flectī spērāre precandō
phrases.english: stop hoping to bend the decrees of the gods by praying

spei.html: De Vaan 580 heads the entry spēs, speī. After a consonant the e of the fifth-declension genitive is short: Lewis & Short itself prints fidĕi, and gives rēi only for Lucretius (s.v. rēs).
